Recipe Converter

Paste a recipe and every line with a known ingredient is converted at once: 2¼ cups all-purpose flour becomes 270 g, ¾ cup brown sugar 160 g. Switch to cups to go the other way.

    How it works

    Each line is read for an amount, a unit and the ingredient, and the ingredient is matched to its weight per cup: flour, sugar, butter, milk and the rest of the 23 ingredients in the kitchen charts. "Flour" is read as all-purpose, "sugar" as granulated and "salt" as fine table salt, which is what most recipes mean. The original amount stays in brackets so you can check it.

    Lines the converter doesn't have a weight for, like vanilla extract or kosher salt, are left as they are and marked, rather than guessed. Eggs and other counted items are left alone. Everything happens in your browser.

    Ingredients it knows

    all-purpose flour, granulated sugar, butter, brown sugar, powdered sugar, water, peanut butter, uncooked white rice, cooked white rice, bread flour, cocoa powder, rolled oats, milk, vegetable oil, sour cream, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cake flour, almond flour, whole wheat flour, honey, chocolate chips.

    Questions

    Why convert a recipe to grams?

    Weighing is faster and more consistent than cups. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 120 to 150 g depending on how it’s scooped; 120 g is always 120 g. It also means fewer measuring cups to wash.

    Why was a line left unchanged?

    Either it has no amount and unit (like "2 eggs" or "pinch of salt"), or the ingredient isn’t one the converter has a weight for. Unknown ingredients are marked instead of guessed.

    Which flour does "flour" mean?

    All-purpose flour, at 120 g per cup spooned and leveled. Bread flour weighs the same; cake flour is a little lighter at about 113 g. Write the flour type in the line to get its exact weight.

    Can it convert grams back to cups?

    Yes. Choose "Cups & spoons" and lines measured in grams, ounces or pounds are converted to cups, tablespoons or teaspoons.
